affected_device: MQTT broker serving ICU infusion pumps (Mosquitto v2.0.15)
observed_behaviour: At 14:22 UTC, the hospital MQTT broker began receiving a sustained stream of malformed PUBLISH packets on the topic /icu/pump/dosage. Network flow analysis later confirmed 5,130 anomalous TCP flows during the 8-minute window, with a peak packet rate of 33,147 packets per second and individual payload sizes reaching 1,514 bytes — exceeding the broker's configured maximum of 512 bytes for clinical telemetry topics. The broker's schema validation module flagged each oversized payload as a protocol violation and logged the event with error code MQTT-4 (malformed packet). No malformed message was forwarded downstream to any infusion pump. Broker CPU rose to 71% during the peak period. All flows were TCP (Protocol Type 6); no UDP traffic was observed, consistent with MQTT-over-TLS operation.
actions_taken: The broker's anomaly threshold — configured at 200 protocol violations per minute — triggered an automated alert to the security operations console at 14:24 UTC. The SOC analyst on duty confirmed the source IP (10.4.2.91) as a compromised nursing workstation in Ward 3B by cross-referencing the SIEM access log. A firewall rule isolating 10.4.2.91 from the IoMT VLAN was applied at 14:28 UTC, terminating the attack flow. All broker event logs were exported to the tamper-evident SIEM within 3 minutes of alert. The workstation was physically isolated and submitted for forensic imaging at 14:45 UTC.
outcome: No ePHI was exposed or altered. The broker's schema validation layer rejected all 5,130 malformed flows before forwarding. Infusion pump dosing continued from the last valid received parameters throughout the incident. Post-incident log review confirmed NTP clock synchronisation was maintained — all broker timestamps align with the SIEM to within 1 second. No patient records were accessed from the compromised workstation during the attack window. Incident classified as Fully Addressed against access control and integrity atoms; audit log atoms confirmed satisfied.

affected_device: MQTT broker serving ward vital-signs monitors (Eclipse Mosquitto)
observed_behaviour: At 02:11 UTC during night shift, the ward MQTT broker received a sequence of malformed CONNECT packets from an external IP that had bypassed the VPN gateway. Flow records show 312 flows over a 104-second window at a mean packet rate of 308 packets per second. Payload sizes were within normal bounds (mean 646 bytes) but the CONNECT packet flags were set incorrectly — the Clean Session flag was absent and the Protocol Name field contained non-UTF-8 bytes, causing the broker to log MQTT protocol parse errors. Unlike INC-013-A, the broker did not have schema validation enabled on the CONNECT handler — only on PUBLISH. The broker accepted three malformed CONNECT sessions before the parse error counter tripped a restart watchdog at 02:13 UTC. During the 2-minute broker outage, 14 vital-sign monitors lost their telemetry connection.
actions_taken: The broker watchdog automatically restarted the service at 02:13 UTC. Night shift staff noticed the monitor disconnection alert on the central nursing station and manually checked on the 14 affected patients. No clinical deterioration was observed. The security team was paged at 02:15 UTC. On-call analyst reviewed broker restart logs and identified the external source IP. A block rule was added at the perimeter firewall at 02:31 UTC. Post-incident review at 07:00 UTC determined that CONNECT-handler schema validation had been inadvertently disabled during a broker configuration update 6 days prior.
outcome: ePHI was not exfiltrated — the malformed CONNECT sessions did not grant the attacker subscriber access to any clinical topic. However, the 2-minute broker outage constitutes a partial failure: 14 devices lost telemetry continuity and the audit log has a gap from 02:13 to 02:13:47 UTC during the broker restart. Integrity atoms partially satisfied — ePHI was not altered but continuity was interrupted. Audit control atom partially satisfied due to the log gap. The missing CONNECT-handler validation is a configuration gap directly attributable to the change management failure.

affected_device: Infusion pump (IP 10.3.1.22) on wired clinical LAN, Ward 5
observed_behaviour: At 10:44 UTC, an attacker connected to a physical Ethernet port in an unlocked equipment room sent gratuitous ARP replies at a peak rate of 153,124 packets per second — consistent with the maximum observed in CICIoMT2024 ARP spoofing flows. The attack poisoned the ARP cache of the Ward 5 network switch, redirecting traffic destined for the clinical gateway (10.3.1.1) through the attacker's laptop (MAC 00:0c:29:3f:aa:12). Network flow analysis recorded 16,047 ARP flows over an 82-second window. The infusion pump at 10.3.1.22 attempted to transmit a TLS-encrypted ePHI dosing record to the clinical server at 10:44:31 UTC. The attacker's machine received the TLS ClientHello but presented a self-signed certificate. The pump's TLS library performed certificate chain validation and rejected the certificate — connection refused with error TLS-CERT-VERIFY-FAIL logged at the pump.
actions_taken: The pump's failed connection attempt generated a local alarm visible to the bedside nurse at 10:44:35 UTC. The nurse contacted the biomedical engineering helpdesk. The network team identified the anomalous ARP traffic on the switch port logs at 10:51 UTC and disabled the physical port (switchport shutdown) at 10:53 UTC. The attacker's device was seized. ARP cache on affected devices was flushed. All clinical devices on Ward 5 re-established their TLS connections to the legitimate gateway within 90 seconds of port shutdown.
outcome: ePHI was not exposed. The TLS certificate validation on the infusion pump rejected the man-in-the-middle certificate, preventing decryption of any clinical payload. The attacker intercepted the encrypted TLS stream for 9 minutes but obtained no readable ePHI. Entity authentication atom fully satisfied — the pump correctly verified the server's identity. Transmission security atom fully satisfied — encryption in transit held under active interception. Physical security atom partially satisfied — the unlocked equipment room enabled the initial physical access.

affected_device: Continuous glucose monitor gateway (IP 10.5.0.8), Endocrinology ward
observed_behaviour: At 23:17 UTC, ARP spoofing traffic was detected originating from a device on the hospital guest Wi-Fi that had accessed the clinical VLAN through a misconfigured VLAN trunk. Flow records consistent with CICIoMT2024 ARP spoofing patterns show 377 packets per second mean rate over a 250-second window, with mixed TCP (52%) and UDP (45%) traffic — indicating the attacker was attempting to intercept both ePHI telemetry (TCP/TLS) and NTP synchronisation (UDP/123). The CGM gateway (10.5.0.8) was running firmware v3.1.2 which did not enforce TLS certificate pinning — it accepted any certificate signed by a root CA in its trust store. The attacker presented a certificate issued by a rogue CA that had been added to the gateway's trust store during a supply chain compromise 3 months prior. The gateway established a full TLS session with the attacker's machine and transmitted 23 minutes of CGM readings before the anomaly was detected.
actions_taken: The hospital SIEM detected the anomalous VLAN traffic at 23:39 UTC and alerted the on-call security engineer. The clinical VLAN was isolated from the guest network at 23:41 UTC by reverting the trunk configuration. The CGM gateway was taken offline at 23:43 UTC. Forensic review identified the rogue CA certificate in the gateway trust store. All CGM gateways of the same model (n=12) were audited; 3 additional units contained the rogue CA. All four were taken offline and replaced with patched units. The VLAN misconfiguration was corrected and access controls reviewed.
outcome: ePHI was exfiltrated. Approximately 23 minutes of CGM readings for one patient were transmitted in plaintext (after TLS termination at the attacker's machine) and captured. Entity authentication atom not satisfied — the gateway accepted a rogue certificate. Transmission security atom not satisfied — ePHI reached an unauthorised party. The incident demonstrates the NA-bias risk: a policy document stating 'TLS is enforced' would be labelled Fully Addressed by a human annotator, but the atom 'the covered entity shall implement procedures to verify that an entity seeking access to ePHI is the one claimed' is Not Addressed at the implementation level.

affected_device: Patient monitoring gateway, Cardiology ICU (IP 10.2.0.5)
observed_behaviour: At 11:03 UTC the cardiology ICU gateway began receiving a distributed TCP SYN flood. Network flow analysis recorded 199,390 TCP flows over a 64-second window at a mean rate of 1,864 packets per second, with a peak of 509,765 pkt/s. SYN flag proportion was 0.87 — confirming a half-open connection flood. The gateway's TCP connection table (configured for 4,096 simultaneous half-open connections) saturated within 8 seconds. Legitimate connections from 11 bedside monitors were refused from 11:03:08 UTC onward. No UDP or ICMP traffic was present — the attack was purely TCP SYN. The gateway continued forwarding previously established, fully authenticated sessions; only new connection attempts were dropped.
actions_taken: The hospital IDS (Snort rule SID-1000045) triggered a DDoS alert at 11:03:12 UTC. The upstream firewall applied a SYN rate-limit of 500 pkt/s per source IP at 11:03:40 UTC. Because the attack was distributed across 34 source IPs, per-IP limiting reduced but did not eliminate the flood. The network team applied a global SYN cookie configuration on the gateway at 11:05:22 UTC, restoring the connection table. All IDS alerts and firewall rule changes were logged to the SIEM with NTP-synchronised timestamps.
outcome: ePHI in already-established sessions was not exposed or interrupted. New monitor connections were refused for 2 minutes 22 seconds. SYN cookie mitigation restored full connectivity at 11:05:22 UTC. Audit logs were intact throughout — the gateway remained operational and continued logging. Access control atoms satisfied for existing sessions; partially satisfied for new connection attempts during the flood window. Audit control atoms fully satisfied.

affected_device: IoMT clinical subnet 10.3.0.0/24 (40 devices)
observed_behaviour: At 22:40 UTC a ping sweep was performed against the entire IoMT subnet 10.3.0.0/24. Flow records: 740 ICMP flows over 20 seconds, mean rate 1,164 pkt/s, peak 118,250 pkt/s. ICMP proportion was 0.02 — the sweep also carried TCP (0.26) and UDP (0.01) probes, consistent with a tool like nmap -sn (ping scan with ARP). The sweep originated from an IP in the hospital's biomedical engineering VLAN (10.8.0.44) — a zone with broader network access than clinical VLANs. Within 20 seconds the attacker had identified 36 of the 40 live IoMT devices. The IDS did not alert — the ping sweep rate (740 flows/20s) fell below the IDS threshold configured for DDoS detection but not for reconnaissance.
actions_taken: The sweep was identified retrospectively during a weekly SIEM log review 4 days later. The biomedical engineering IP was traced to a contractor laptop. The contractor was interviewed; they stated the scan was conducted to 'check which devices were online' without authorisation. Network access controls were reviewed and the biomedical VLAN's route to the IoMT subnet was restricted to specific management ports only. The IDS reconnaissance detection threshold was lowered.
outcome: No ePHI was accessed — a ping sweep returns only liveness information, not data. However, the attacker obtained a live device map of 36 IoMT devices. This reconnaissance preceded a targeted port scan 6 days later (see INC-012-A). The 4-day detection lag means the access control atom is not satisfied — unauthorised lateral movement was not detected in real time. Event logging atom partially satisfied — the sweep was logged but not reviewed in time to prevent follow-on reconnaissance.
