affected_device: Radiology PACS gateway node (Infinitt PACS v4.2), single-NIC server
observed_behaviour: At 11:15 UTC, the PACS gateway's TCP stack began receiving SYN segments from a single external IP (203.0.113.77) at a sustained rate of approximately 28,400 half-open connections over a 6-minute window, yielding 31,742 observed network flows. The server's SYN backlog queue (default 128 entries) saturated within 4 seconds, causing three radiology workstations to time out while attempting to retrieve DICOM images for active CT studies. Server-side logs recorded 'connection refused' on port 104 (DICOM) starting at 11:15:04 UTC. Packet capture confirmed the attack source used no IP spoofing — all SYN segments arrived from the same /32 address. No authentication exchange was attempted; the server never reached the ESTABLISHED state for any malicious connection. ePHI stored within the PACS database remained accessible from the internal DICOM router throughout the incident.
actions_taken: The network IDS (Snort 3.1, rule SID 1-10001) triggered a DoS alert at 11:16 UTC after the SYN rate exceeded its 5,000-half-open threshold. The SOC applied an ACL on the perimeter firewall blocking 203.0.113.77 at 11:18 UTC, after which SYN traffic ceased immediately. The SYN backlog cleared within 90 seconds; all three radiology workstations re-established DICOM connections by 11:21 UTC. A forensic copy of the IDS alert and firewall ACL change log was written to the SIEM. The treating radiologists were notified of the 6-minute retrieval delay; no clinical decision was deferred.
outcome: Attack contained. SYN backlog exhausted for 6 minutes, causing retrieval delays, but no ePHI was accessed or disclosed. DICOM service restored at 11:21 UTC. Firewall ACL in place. Source IP blocked.

affected_device: Telemetry aggregation server for step-down cardiac unit (6-bed), Dell PowerEdge R640
observed_behaviour: At 02:07 UTC, the cardiac telemetry server's listener on port 8443 began receiving SYN segments from a single IP (198.51.100.202) at approximately 9,800 half-open connections per minute. The attack sustained for 22 minutes, generating 38,914 observed flows before the source ceased. SYN cookie support was disabled on this server (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0, confirmed in post-incident audit) because an older firmware version of the bedside telemetry transmitter required traditional SYN-ACK handshake semantics. The server's listen backlog exhausted at 02:07:19 UTC; subsequent legitimate TCP connections from bedside monitors were dropped silently. Clinical nursing staff noticed absence of real-time waveforms on the central console at 02:09 UTC. The unit reverted to manual vital-sign observation per documented backup protocol, but two patients missed scheduled automated SpO2 alarms at 02:14 and 02:19 UTC that would have triggered nurse alerts for SpO2 < 92%. Both patients were physically checked by the on-duty nurse at 02:22 UTC (no adverse outcome documented). ePHI telemetry buffered on the bedside devices was not transmitted for the 22-minute outage window.
actions_taken: The NOC duty engineer received a pager alert at 02:09 UTC (server CPU idle, connection count anomaly). Manual firewall rule blocking 198.51.100.202 was applied at 02:19 UTC. The server TCP stack recovered by 02:24 UTC; telemetry stream resumed. Buffered ePHI from bedside monitors was re-transmitted and ingested at 02:24–02:31 UTC. The post-incident report noted the missing SYN cookie configuration as a contributing factor. The configuration was remediated (tcp_syncookies=1 + updated firmware) during a maintenance window on 2024-08-23.
outcome: Telemetry unavailable for 22 minutes. ePHI in transit (SpO2, ECG waveforms) was not delivered during the outage window; buffered data was recovered post-incident. No exfiltration occurred, but two automated alarm events were missed during the disruption. Configuration remediation completed 2024-08-23.

affected_device: Insulin pump management server (CareLink v3.5.1, Medtronic OEM)
observed_behaviour: At 16:44 UTC, the insulin pump management server's REST API endpoint (TCP/443) received a fully-established TCP flood from a single compromised host (10.8.1.55) within the hospital's guest Wi-Fi VLAN. The attacker maintained 214 simultaneous ESTABLISHED connections, each sending empty HTTP/1.1 keep-alive frames at 1,200 requests per second, generating 44,182 observed flows over a 9-minute attack window with a peak throughput of 89,400 packets per second. The server's thread pool (200 worker threads, Tomcat 9.0.65) saturated at 16:44:38 UTC, causing HTTP 503 responses for legitimate insulin dose-confirmation requests from pump devices on the clinical VLAN. No injection into the clinical data path was observed — the attacker's traffic remained on the REST API surface, and ePHI held in the Oracle DB backend was not queried or exfiltrated.
actions_taken: The hospital's network access control system flagged 10.8.1.55 (a guest VLAN IP) for unusual east-west traffic at 16:46 UTC. The NOC applied a VLAN ACL blocking the guest VLAN from reaching the clinical server subnet at 16:49 UTC, dropping all 214 connections. Thread pool utilisation fell to 3% within 45 seconds. Audit logs from the server's access log (rotated to SIEM hourly) confirmed no ePHI records were returned to 10.8.1.55 during the incident. The server's web application firewall (ModSecurity CRS 3.3) was enabled post-incident to limit per-IP connection counts.
outcome: No ePHI was accessed or exfiltrated. Pump dose-confirmation responses were unavailable for 5 minutes; clinical staff used bedside device confirmation as fallback. Service restored fully at 16:53 UTC.

affected_device: Real-time location system (RTLS) gateway for medical asset tracking (Zebra ZL10)
observed_behaviour: At 20:53 UTC, the RTLS gateway's UDP listener on port 5000 received a volumetric flood from a single IP (172.16.88.23, later attributed to a compromised biomedical engineering workstation). The flood comprised 67,813 observed flows over 11 minutes at a mean rate of 1,412 packets per second and peak of 183,040 packets per second. Each UDP datagram was 256 bytes, well-formed but carrying random payload content unrecognised by the RTLS protocol parser. The gateway's inbound buffer (16 MB) overflowed at 20:53:42 UTC, causing it to drop incoming location beacons from 34 tagged infusion pumps, 12 defibrillators, and 7 ventilators. Clinical staff lost real-time location visibility for those assets for 8 minutes. No ePHI was processed by the RTLS gateway itself — asset tags transmitted device IDs and location coordinates only, not patient data.
actions_taken: Network monitoring detected the UDP spike at 20:55 UTC via a NetFlow anomaly rule (>1,000% baseline). A firewall rate-limiting rule capping UDP on port 5000 to 500 pkt/s per source IP was applied at 20:59 UTC. The gateway rebooted automatically at 21:01 UTC per its watchdog timer; asset visibility was restored at 21:03 UTC after beacon re-registration. 172.16.88.23 was isolated and submitted for forensic analysis. Post-incident the biomed VLAN was segregated from the RTLS subnet.
outcome: No ePHI exposed. Asset location data unavailable for 8 minutes. Clinical impact: staff located devices manually; no care delay documented. Gateway recovered via watchdog reboot at 21:01 UTC.

affected_device: Pulse oximeter gateway (Nonin WristOx2 aggregator), embedded Linux 4.19
observed_behaviour: At 03:28 UTC, the pulse oximeter gateway experienced an ICMP echo-request flood from 10.2.4.109 (a nurse call station running legacy Windows 7 that was compromised via a phishing link). A total of 23,914 observed flows were recorded over 7 minutes at a mean packet rate of 814 packets per second and peak of 41,209 packets per second. The gateway's network stack allocated interrupt processing time to ICMP responses, crowding out the TCP listener on port 9001 that forwards SpO2 readings to the EHR. SpO2 transmission from six bedside oximeters dropped for 7 minutes (03:28–03:35 UTC). A post-incident EHR audit found that SpO2 readings for two patients — with documented respiratory conditions — had gaps of 7 and 9 minutes respectively in their continuous monitoring records. A nurse physically checked both patients during the gap; no adverse clinical event was documented. However, the missing readings were not flagged in the audit log at the time of occurrence — the EHR assumed connection loss and silently discarded the gap rather than raising an alarm.
actions_taken: The NOC received an automated EHR connectivity alert at 03:31 UTC (3-minute delay from event start). The perimeter firewall ICMP rate-limit rule (50 pkt/s per host, already in place) had not been applied to the IoMT internal subnet — a configuration oversight. A blanket ICMP rate-limit was applied network-wide at 03:36 UTC. The gateway recovered without restart at 03:35 UTC as the flood ceased. Logs from the compromised nurse call station were imaged. The EHR vendor was notified of the silent-gap behaviour and issued a configuration update to raise an alert for SpO2 gaps > 2 minutes.
outcome: SpO2 telemetry unavailable for 7 minutes for 6 patients; records contain 7–9 minute gaps. No ePHI was exfiltrated. Silent EHR gap handling was a partial control failure — the absence of a gap alarm is documented as a finding. Remediated: ICMP rate-limit extended to internal IoMT subnet; EHR alert threshold set to 2 minutes.

affected_device: MQTT broker for neonatal ICU (NICU) remote monitoring (HiveMQ 4.12), 8-bed unit
observed_behaviour: At 10:08 UTC, the HiveMQ broker began receiving CONNECT packets at a rate far exceeding normal device registration. Network flow analysis captured 12,773 TCP flows over a 64-second burst, with a mean flow rate of 344.6 packets per second and a peak of 236,841 packets per second — all originating from a single internal IP (10.5.3.202, later identified as a misconfigured load-testing tool left running by a biomedical IT trainee). Each CONNECT packet presented a unique client ID string (randomly generated, 23-character alphanumeric), exhausting the broker's in-flight CONNECT concurrency limit of 5,000 within 2 seconds. The broker logged 'Connection limit exceeded' at 10:08:02 UTC and began queuing then dropping CONNECT attempts. Legitimate NICU devices (12 registered pulse oximeters and 8 respiration monitors) lost their MQTT sessions and were unable to reconnect for 43 seconds. Mean inter-arrival time across flows was approximately 84.6 ms, consistent with a single machine generating connections in a tight loop.
actions_taken: The HiveMQ management API raised a 'connection-rate overload' alert at 10:08:05 UTC. The biomedical IT supervisor on call identified 10.5.3.202 as the source within 2 minutes and terminated the load-testing process at 10:10 UTC. NICU devices began automatic MQTT reconnection (QoS 1 persistent sessions) immediately after the source ceased; all 20 devices had restored sessions by 10:11 UTC. Broker logs and the network flow capture were archived to the SIEM. A post-incident change control record was filed noting that load-testing tools must not be run on the clinical MQTT broker VLAN.
outcome: No ePHI was exposed or lost. NICU device telemetry interrupted for 43 seconds; QoS 1 persistent sessions preserved buffered readings on device side. No clinical adverse event. Incident root cause: unauthorised load test on clinical infrastructure.

affected_device: MQTT broker for remote patient monitoring (RPM) portal, 38 enrolled home-care patients
observed_behaviour: At 23:41 UTC, the RPM MQTT broker received a CONNECT flood from 203.0.113.55, an external IP geolocated to a commercial VPS provider. The flood produced 11,904 flows over approximately 58 seconds with a peak connection-request rate of 198,730 per second — consistent with the CICIoMT2024 Connect Flood profile. The broker was running EMQ X 4.4.18 with the anonymous-access plugin enabled (a temporary measure applied two weeks prior for a vendor integration test that was never reverted). Anonymous CONNECT packets were accepted without credential validation, allowing the attacker to establish up to 200 simultaneous sessions before the broker's open-connections limit was reached. Legitimate patient devices — glucose meters and SpO2 rings belonging to 38 home-care patients — were evicted from their MQTT sessions by the broker's LRU eviction policy as the connection table filled. The broker's topic ACL was not enforced for anonymous clients in the active configuration; the attacker's sessions had read access to all retained messages on /rpm/# topics, which included the last 30 minutes of SpO2 and blood glucose readings for each enrolled patient.
actions_taken: The RPM platform's on-call alert fired at 23:43 UTC when patient device reconnection failures exceeded 50%. The incident responder identified the anonymous plugin as the root cause at 23:51 UTC and disabled it, requiring all clients to present credentials. Attacker sessions were terminated immediately. A forensic export of broker session logs was taken; the broker's retained-message store for /rpm/# was audited for evidence of SUBSCRIBE commands from the attacker's sessions. Log analysis confirmed 14 SUBSCRIBE packets targeting /rpm/+/glucose and /rpm/+/spo2, meaning the attacker received retained ePHI for up to 38 patients during the 10-minute window. The hospital's privacy officer was notified at 01:15 UTC the following day; a HIPAA breach notification process was initiated.
outcome: ePHI disclosed: up to 38 patients' last-30-minute SpO2 and blood glucose retained messages exposed to external attacker due to anonymous MQTT access. Incident classified as a reportable HIPAA breach. Anonymous plugin permanently disabled. All patient devices re-enrolled with unique MQTT credentials issued from the HSM-backed credential store.
attck_technique: T0814 — Denial of Service / T0817 — Modify Alarm Settings (indirect: device eviction silenced alarms)

affected_device: MQTT broker for surgical suite physiologic monitoring gateway (Philips IntelliVue MX800 integration layer)
observed_behaviour: At 08:33 UTC, the surgical suite MQTT broker received a PUBLISH flood from client ID 'svc-integration-05' — a legitimate service account whose credential had been obtained by a rogue vendor remote-support session the prior day. The attacker published to topic /or/suite3/monitor/vitals at a rate of approximately 507.6 messages per second (consistent with the CICIoMT2024 DoS Publish Flood profile mean), sustaining 44,376 observed flows over 64 minutes. Individual PUBLISH payloads ranged from 128 bytes to 505,197 bytes (max observed in the dataset: 505,197-byte PUBLISH), with mean header length 48,670 bytes. The broker's message-rate limiter (set at 1,000 msg/s per client) was not breached, but the downstream subscriber — a Python bridge process forwarding OR vitals to the anaesthesia EHR — became I/O-bound processing the large payloads. The bridge process's queue depth reached 100,000 messages at 08:41 UTC and began dropping the oldest messages to prevent OOM. Genuine IntelliVue MX800 telemetry (HR, SpO2, EtCO2) was among the dropped messages between 08:41 and 08:53 UTC.
actions_taken: The anaesthesia EHR integration team received an alert at 08:44 UTC (queue-depth alarm on the bridge process). The security team revoked credentials for 'svc-integration-05' at 08:48 UTC, immediately ending the PUBLISH flood. The bridge process queue drained by 08:53 UTC and resumed delivering legitimate OR telemetry. An audit of MQTT ACLs identified that 'svc-integration-05' had publish rights on /or/# with no payload-size restriction. Post-incident: payload-size limits of 8 KB were configured for all service accounts on OR topics; the vendor remote-support session policy was updated to require dual approval.
outcome: Genuine OR telemetry (HR, SpO2, EtCO2) dropped between 08:41–08:53 UTC during a live surgical case. No ePHI was exfiltrated — attacker's PUBLISH payloads were random bytes with no subscriber retrieving patient data. Telemetry gaps were filled from the IntelliVue bedside store retrospectively. Anaesthesiologist documented awareness of the monitoring interruption in the operative note.

affected_device: MQTT broker for ward-level EHR synchronisation (32 beds, mixed medical/surgical)
observed_behaviour: At 17:22 UTC, a Publish Flood originated from client 'device-update-svc' — a compromised OTA firmware updater — targeting topic /ward/+/ehr/sync. Network analysis captured 38,914 flows over 55 minutes at a mean rate of 621.4 msg/s and peak of 840,826 msg/s (consistent with the CICIoMT2024 DoS Publish Flood peak). Payload sizes ranged from 1 to 505,197 bytes. The MQTT broker (Mosquitto 2.0.15) applied no payload cap; the ward EHR sync subscriber consumed messages without rate control. By 17:31 UTC the subscriber's write queue had grown to 48 GB of unprocessed payloads, consuming all available disk on the EHR sync node and causing the node's PostgreSQL write-ahead log to halt. The EHR sync node stopped processing inbound ward records at 17:31 UTC. For the 31-minute window (17:31–18:02 UTC) nurse-station entries (medication administration records, vitals charted manually) were queued locally on ward terminals but not yet persisted to the EHR backend. No ePHI was actively exfiltrated; however, the attacker's wildcard topic subscription (+) allowed the 'device-update-svc' client to SUBSCRIBE to /ward/+/ehr/sync and receive 14 minutes of legitimate sync payloads (17:22–17:36 UTC) before the SOC revoked the credential — these payloads contained ePHI.
actions_taken: SOC identified disk exhaustion alert at 17:33 UTC. Credential for 'device-update-svc' was revoked at 17:36 UTC. EHR sync node disk was cleared and PostgreSQL WAL restarted at 17:58 UTC; queued ward records flushed and committed by 18:02 UTC. Forensic log review confirmed 14 minutes of ePHI delivery to the attacker's subscription before revocation. HIPAA breach notification process initiated. Post-incident: Mosquitto ACL configured to deny SUBSCRIBE on /ward/# for OTA service accounts; all OTA service accounts limited to publish on /ota/# only.
outcome: Partial breach: ePHI (ward medication and vitals sync payloads) received by attacker's SUBSCRIBE session for 14 minutes before credential revocation. EHR sync unavailable 31 minutes; no records lost, only delayed. Breach notification filed under 45 CFR §164.400.
attck_technique: T0814 — Denial of Service / T0830 — Adversary-in-the-Middle (passive SUBSCRIBE interception)

affected_device: Clinical data repository gateway (CDR) serving ICU telemetry archive, dual-homed server
observed_behaviour: At 04:18 UTC, a distributed TCP flood from 47 source IPs (botnet, geographically spread across 12 countries) targeted the CDR gateway's HTTPS port (443) and DICOM port (104) simultaneously. Network telemetry captured 202,311 flows — matching the CICIoMT2024 DDoS-TCP profile — with a peak throughput of 2,097,152 packets per second sustained for 19 minutes. Both listeners became unresponsive at 04:18:41 UTC. The CDR gateway operated a legacy read replica of the ICU ePHI archive (last 90 days of telemetry) that was configured with HTTP basic authentication on an internal management port (8080) — this port was inadvertently exposed to the internet via a misconfigured NAT rule. During the DDoS window, an external actor (separate from the flood source — likely opportunistic scanning) made 14 authenticated HTTP GET requests to port 8080 between 04:23 and 04:31 UTC, retrieving 14 DICOM metadata records (patient name, MRN, study date) before the NOC detected the open port and closed the NAT rule.
actions_taken: Upstream ISP null-route applied at 04:27 UTC after the NOC contacted the DDoS mitigation service (Cloudflare Magic Transit). CDR gateway recovered at 04:39 UTC. A concurrent port-scan sweep by an unrelated actor exploited the confusion window and the open management port. The NAT misconfiguration was identified during post-incident forensics; the management port had been exposed for 11 days before the incident. Fourteen DICOM metadata records were confirmed retrieved; the CDR vendor was engaged to determine whether any additional queries were possible within the 14-request session log. HIPAA breach notification process initiated for 14 patient records.
outcome: 14 patient DICOM metadata records (name, MRN, study date) exfiltrated via the inadvertently exposed management interface during the DDoS disruption window. DDoS itself caused 21 minutes of telemetry archive unavailability. Breach notification filed. Management port permanently closed; NAT rules audited enterprise-wide.
attck_technique: T0814 — Denial of Service / T0886 — Remote Services (opportunistic exploitation of exposed management port during DDoS)

affected_device: Central patient monitoring hub (Philips IntelliSpace, 24-bed ICU), dual-core embedded appliance
observed_behaviour: At 01:55 UTC during a minimal-staffing night shift, 194,938 observed flows of ICMP echo requests arrived from 39 distributed source IPs across 9 ASNs, with a mean packet rate of 483,110 packets per second and a peak of 1,321,810 packets per second (matching the CICIoMT2024 DDoS-ICMP1 profile). The IntelliSpace appliance's kernel interrupt handler consumed 94% of both CPU cores within 8 seconds of the onset, rendering the appliance unable to respond to NTP synchronisation packets. By 01:55:22 UTC the system clock drifted 4.2 seconds from UTC, causing TLS certificate validation failures against the EHR's strict time-window check (±3 seconds). The TLS failure caused the monitoring appliance's ePHI data export process to abort; however, the export had already transmitted 4 minutes of batched telemetry (covering 24 patients) to the EHR before the connection dropped. The SIEM received no events from the appliance for the 17-minute outage window because the syslog daemon was also starved of CPU cycles. On restoration, the SIEM audit gap was not flagged as a potential HIPAA audit control gap until 5 days later in the weekly log review.
actions_taken: The upstream network team applied ICMP rate-limiting at the ISP edge at 02:09 UTC. The IntelliSpace appliance's network stack recovered at 02:12 UTC and NTP re-synced at 02:14 UTC, restoring TLS connectivity. A 17-minute SIEM gap was discovered during weekly log review on 2024-07-09. The post-incident review noted: (1) ICMP was not rate-limited at the hospital border router; (2) the monitoring appliance had no hardware-based watchdog to alert on syslog silence. Both gaps were remediated in the subsequent change window.
outcome: The 17-minute SIEM blackout represents an audit control gap — activity in an ePHI-handling system was not recorded for 17 minutes, violating HIPAA §164.312(b) Audit Controls. No direct ePHI exfiltration confirmed; however, the absence of audit logs means the absence-of-breach cannot be positively asserted. Clinical monitoring unavailable for 17 minutes; nursing staff used manual observation.

affected_device: VoIP-over-UDP gateway for nurse call system (Rauland 5 integration, port UDP/5060)
observed_behaviour: At 22:14 UTC, a distributed UDP flood targeting port 5060 (SIP/VoIP) produced 206,170 observed flows from 52 source IPs at a mean rate of 741,818 packets per second (peak: 3,294,967 pkt/s — consistent with the CICIoMT2024 DDoS-UDP1 profile). The nurse call gateway, which routes audio and alert signals for a 48-bed ward, became unreachable within 3 seconds. For the 28-minute outage, nurse call alerts (including one bed-exit alarm for a fall-risk patient and two cardiac monitor alarms) could not reach the mobile devices used by ward nurses. Both cardiac alarms were for patients whose telemetry was still being transmitted via a separate TCP path to the EHR, but the nurse notification leg failed. At 22:31 UTC a fall-risk patient (no nurse response to bed-exit alarm) got out of bed unsupervised and fell, sustaining a non-life-threatening wrist fracture. The patient's identifiable incident report — including name, MRN, injury details — was filed in the EHR immediately. The fall incident report is ePHI and its creation was prompted by the attacker-induced alarm failure, establishing a direct causal chain.
actions_taken: NOC applied ACL blocking the 52 source IPs at 22:18 UTC; the flood resumed from 4 new IPs at 22:24 UTC before the ISP null-route took effect at 22:32 UTC. Service restored at 22:42 UTC. The patient fall was reported to the hospital's risk management office. A post-incident review established that the SIP gateway had no failover to a wired nurse call path during network outage. A hardware-based nurse call backup (direct-wired panel) was activated after the incident as an interim measure.
outcome: One patient fall directly attributable to alarm failure during DDoS outage; fall incident report (ePHI) created. Network-level ePHI exfiltration: none. Causal harm: patient injury and associated ePHI creation due to failed nurse notification controls. Alarm-path redundancy remediated post-incident.
attck_technique: T0814 — Denial of Service / T0817 — Modify Alarm Settings (indirect: alarm delivery path silenced)

affected_device: Medication dispensing cabinet network interface (Omnicell XR2, TCP/443 management API)
observed_behaviour: At 14:03 UTC, a sustained TCP flood from 10.11.0.44 (a rogue device connected to the clinical Wi-Fi via a hidden access point discovered later) produced 51,847 observed flows over 17 minutes at a mean rate of 63,210 packets per second. The dispensing cabinet's management API, running on an embedded ARM SoC with 512 MB RAM, exhausted its TCP connection pool (maximum 256 connections) at 14:03:18 UTC. Pharmacists were unable to remotely verify cabinet inventory or override a locked medication drawer via the management portal. At 14:07 UTC, a pharmacist manually opened the cabinet using the physical key override, but the override did not log to the management system because the logging daemon was also stalled awaiting TCP stack resources. Two manual medication pulls (morphine 4 mg IV, lorazepam 2 mg) were performed and documented only on paper during the 17-minute window — the paper records were not transferred to the EHR until 14:39 UTC. Controlled substance dispensing without electronic logging for 17 minutes constitutes a gap in the electronic audit trail required under HIPAA and DEA 21 CFR Part 1304.
actions_taken: NOC isolated 10.11.0.44 at 14:19 UTC by disabling the switch port. Cabinet management API recovered at 14:21 UTC; electronic logging resumed. Paper-based medication records were entered into the EHR at 14:39 UTC by the pharmacy supervisor. A controlled substance discrepancy audit was initiated. The rogue access point (a commercial consumer router) was physically recovered and submitted for forensic examination. Post-incident: the clinical Wi-Fi now enforces 802.1X authentication with certificate-based device identity.
outcome: Electronic audit trail for two controlled substance dispenses missing for 17 minutes. No patient ePHI was transmitted externally. Compliance gap: DEA 21 CFR Part 1304 and HIPAA §164.312(b) audit controls. Remediation: 802.1X authentication on clinical Wi-Fi; paper-to-EHR reconciliation policy enacted within 30 minutes of any outage.

affected_device: IoMT subnet /22 (1,024 addresses), including 6 ventilators, 14 infusion pumps, 8 CGM bridges
observed_behaviour: At 03:14 UTC, 740 observed ICMP echo-request flows swept the IoMT /22 subnet from 10.99.0.11 (later attributed to a compromised building automation controller). The sweep used a mean flow rate of 1,164.2 packets per second (peak 118,249.9 pkt/s) and completed within 38 seconds, mapping 312 live hosts. The sweep was not detected — the IDS ICMP sweep rule (SID 1-478) had been suppressed for the IoMT VLAN to reduce alert fatigue from legitimate network health probes. No alert was raised. Three days later (2024-05-21), the same compromised controller issued targeted SYN probes to the 312 live hosts, then exploited an unpatched Telnet service (CVE-2019-16028) on an infusion pump identified in the sweep. The attacker extracted dosing configuration files containing 14 patient MRNs and current medication regimens from the pump's onboard flash storage. The ping sweep itself caused no ePHI exposure — the subsequent exploitation did.
actions_taken: The breach was discovered on 2024-05-24 during a routine vulnerability scan that identified the Telnet service. Forensic analysis of the building automation controller's logs established the causal chain from the ping sweep to the exploitation. The ICMP sweep rule suppression was reversed immediately. CVE-2019-16028 was patched on all affected pump models within 72 hours of discovery. A HIPAA breach notification was filed for the 14 patients whose data was extracted.
outcome: Ping sweep itself: no direct ePHI exposure. Subsequent exploitation (enabled by the undetected sweep) resulted in exfiltration of 14 patient medication records. Root cause: IDS rule suppression eliminated detection of the reconnaissance phase. Breach notification filed under 45 CFR §164.400.
attck_technique: T0840 — Network Sniffing / T0888 — Remote Services Exploitation (consequent)

affected_device: ECG monitor fleet (12 devices, Philips PageWriter TC70), management VLAN
observed_behaviour: At 10:29 UTC, 2,173 observed flows targeting the ECG monitor management VLAN originated from 172.20.4.88 — a biomedical engineering workstation running an unauthorised copy of Nessus Essentials (free tier, not approved for clinical VLANs). The scan used a mean rate of 97.5 packets per second (peak 11,401.6 pkt/s) and ran for 22 minutes. Nessus identified 7 open ports across the 12 ECG monitors; 4 devices responded to authenticated SNMP v2c queries using the community string 'public', which was the factory default still in use. The SNMP responses included device serial numbers, firmware version strings, and the MAC address of the primary network interface — no ePHI was stored in SNMP MIBs. However, the firmware version disclosed (FW 2.1.4) matched a known vulnerable version for CVE-2023-44748 (unauthenticated memory-read via a malformed SOAP request). The biomed engineer who ran the scan reported the findings to the IT security team, who did not initially act on the CVE because it was rated CVSS 5.9.
actions_taken: The scan activity was detected in the NDR console as an anomalous flow-rate event 4 days later during regular review. The biomed engineer was interviewed and disclosed the scan was intentional but unapproved. The SNMP community string was changed from 'public' to a random 32-character string on all 12 devices. CVE-2023-44748 was reassessed in context — the IoMT VLAN exposure raised the effective risk — and a firmware update was applied within 14 days. A policy addendum requiring IT Security approval for any network scanning on clinical VLANs was issued.
outcome: No ePHI exposed during the scan itself. Partial control gap: factory-default SNMP community string ('public') enabled unauthenticated enumeration of device firmware versions, facilitating future CVE identification by an adversary. CVE remediated. Unauthorised scanning on clinical VLAN addressed in policy.
attck_technique: T0888 — Remote Services Exploitation (pre-stage) / T0842 — Network Sniffing

affected_device: Patient wearable gateway cluster (3 nodes, Raspberry Pi 4B running Raspberry Pi OS Bullseye)
observed_behaviour: At 06:47 UTC, 16,832 observed network flows from an external IP (185.220.101.4, a Tor exit node) swept the demilitarised zone containing patient wearable gateways at a mean rate of 148.1 packets per second (peak 90,366.6 pkt/s) over 29 minutes. The OS fingerprinting scan identified all three gateways as 'Linux 5.10 (Raspbian)' based on TCP window size, TTL, and SYN option field analysis. The gateways were directly internet-accessible on port 22 (SSH) — a configuration left in place for vendor remote support. The attacker correlated the OS fingerprint with public exploit databases and identified CVE-2022-0847 (Dirty Pipe, Linux kernel ≤5.16.11 privilege escalation). Within 6 hours of the OS scan, the attacker connected to one gateway via SSH using a credential spray (the default username 'pi' with password 'raspberry' was in use on one of the three nodes). Local privilege escalation via Dirty Pipe succeeded; the attacker installed a reverse shell. Wearable telemetry (heart rate, SpO2, activity data) for 19 enrolled rehabilitation patients was accessible from the compromised gateway's local data cache.
actions_taken: The compromise was discovered on 2024-07-24 by the SIEM detecting outbound reverse-shell traffic. The compromised node was isolated immediately. Forensic analysis established the OS scan as the reconnaissance step. All three gateways were patched to Linux 5.15.85 (Dirty Pipe fix). SSH default credentials were changed to certificate-based authentication. Internet-direct SSH access was revoked; vendor access now routed through an MFA-protected jump server. A breach notification was filed for 19 patients.
outcome: 19 patients' wearable telemetry (HR, SpO2, activity) accessible from the compromised gateway for approximately 48 hours. Breach confirmed. Root cause chain: OS fingerprint disclosed → CVE identified → credential spray succeeded → Dirty Pipe privilege escalation → data access. All three control failures preceded the OS scan detection.
attck_technique: T0888 — Remote Services Exploitation / T0861 — Point-to-Point Encryption Attack

affected_device: IoMT DMZ segment (48 devices, purpose-built network segment with allowlist firewall)
observed_behaviour: At 19:41 UTC, 83,981 observed network flows from 91.108.56.4 (Shodan crawlers, confirmed by reverse DNS and Shodan attribution header in HTTP probes) scanned the IoMT DMZ segment's entire /24 address space across all 65,535 TCP ports over 94 minutes. Mean flow rate was 88.8 packets per second (peak 141,582.6 pkt/s). The segment's allowlist firewall (Palo Alto PA-820, application-default policy) responded with TCP RST for all ports not explicitly permitted; SYN-ACK responses were observed only on ports 443 (HTTPS management), 8883 (MQTT/TLS), and 2000 (DICOM). The scanner received only these three service banners. TLS on all three ports returned certificates issued by the hospital's internal CA, with no hostname or ePHI in the Subject or SANs fields. No authentication was attempted and no vulnerability probes followed the port scan during the 48-hour monitoring window post-scan.
actions_taken: The NDR console (Darktrace) flagged the scan at 19:43 UTC as a 'high-volume external reconnaissance' event. The SOC reviewed and confirmed the source as Shodan (non-targeted passive indexing). No immediate threat response was required beyond logging. The firewall policy was confirmed correct. The SOC added the scan event to the monthly threat landscape report. No credentials, ePHI, or internal service information was disclosed.
outcome: Scan contained. Only three ports disclosed (443, 8883, 2000), all expected. No ePHI accessible. No authentication bypass attempted. Allowlist firewall operated as designed. Logged and documented. No remediation required.

affected_device: MQTT broker for glucose monitoring fleet (27 CGM sensors, Dexcom G7 integration gateway)
observed_behaviour: At 09:05 UTC, the CGM integration gateway received 5,130 malformed MQTT PUBLISH packets — matching the CICIoMT2024 MQTT-Malformed_Data flow count — from 10.3.7.92 (a compromised pharmacy workstation) targeting topic /cgm/+/glucose. Each PUBLISH packet included a malformed remaining-length field (0xFFFFFFFF, maximum 4-byte value encoding) that triggered a heap buffer overflow in the gateway's MQTT parsing library (EMQ X plugin v3.4.12, unpatched). The overflow corrupted 32 bytes of heap memory adjacent to the MQTT session table, overwriting the `client_id` field for three legitimate CGM sensor sessions with attacker-controlled bytes. The three corrupted sessions were re-registered under attacker-controlled client IDs, which gained SUBSCRIBE access to the /cgm/+/glucose topic without credential verification. Over the following 12 minutes the attacker's hijacked sessions received real-time glucose readings for three patients. The payload of each received message included patient device serial number (directly mappable to patient identity via the hospital's device registry) and glucose value in mg/dL.
actions_taken: The anomaly was discovered at 09:19 UTC when a CGM nurse alerted that three sensor devices showed as 'disconnected' in the nursing portal despite physically transmitting data. The SOC correlated the session table corruption with the malformed-packet burst. EMQ X was restarted with the vulnerable plugin disabled at 09:21 UTC; all three patient sessions were re-established with verified credentials. The pharmacy workstation was isolated. Fourteen minutes of glucose readings (09:05–09:19 UTC) for three patients were received by the attacker's sessions — confirmed via broker topic-delivery logs. HIPAA breach notification filed for three patients.
outcome: Heap overflow via malformed MQTT REMAIN-LENGTH field corrupted session table, enabling three unauthenticated SUBSCRIBE hijacks. 14 minutes of real-time glucose ePHI (patient-identifiable via device serial) disclosed to attacker. Breach confirmed for 3 patients. EMQ X plugin updated and heap-allocation hardening (ASLR + canary) verified enabled post-incident.
attck_technique: T0888 — Remote Services Exploitation (heap overflow via malformed protocol message)

affected_device: MQTT broker cluster (2-node HiveMQ 4.14, active-active) for hospital-wide IoMT backbone, 340 registered devices
observed_behaviour: At 07:16 UTC, 41,208 observed MQTT CONNECT flows arrived from 18 geographically distributed source IPs across 5 ASNs, consistent with a botnet-coordinated MQTT DDoS-Connect Flood (estimated 3× the CICIoMT2024 DoS-Connect profile, extrapolated to distributed sources). Peak connection-request rate reached approximately 711,000 per second across both broker nodes. The HiveMQ cluster's connection-rate limiter (configured at 5,000 CONNECT/s per node, global limit 10,000/s) engaged at 07:16:04 UTC, queuing then dropping excess CONNECT attempts. Registered IoMT devices that lost their sessions during the flood automatically retried with exponential back-off (MQTT QoS 1, clean-session=false); all 340 devices re-established sessions within 90 seconds of the flood subsiding. No CONNECT packet presented valid credentials — all used random or null username/password fields that were rejected by the broker's authentication plugin before any session was opened.
actions_taken: The HiveMQ cluster's Prometheus metrics (published to Grafana) triggered a 'connection-rate spike' PagerDuty alert at 07:16:10 UTC. The SOC applied upstream BGP blackholing for the 18 source IPs at 07:22 UTC, ending the flood. Broker logs confirmed zero successful authentications from the attack IPs. QoS 1 message queues for all 340 devices were intact — no telemetry data was lost. A post-incident review confirmed the connection-rate limiter and authentication plugin were operating correctly.
outcome: No ePHI was exposed or lost. MQTT session disruptions resolved within 90 seconds via QoS 1 reconnection. Broker cluster held under connection-rate limiting. Attack duration: 6 minutes. Zero successful attacker authentications.

affected_device: MQTT broker for remote ICU (eICU) telemetry platform, serving 22 off-site critical care beds
observed_behaviour: At 01:48 UTC, a MQTT DDoS Connect Flood — 38,970 observed flows from 24 source IPs at a peak rate of 598,412 CONNECT requests per second — targeted the eICU MQTT broker (Eclipse Mosquitto 2.0.15 with a custom Python authentication plugin). The Python auth plugin, blocking on bcrypt hash verification for each CONNECT request, became CPU-saturated within 4 seconds: each bcrypt call consumed 120 ms at cost factor 12, and 598,000 concurrent requests saturated the 8-core broker host. The authentication plugin's thread pool (32 threads) was exhausted; incoming CONNECT requests began failing silently — critically, both attack CONNECTs and legitimate device CONNECTs failed without rejection codes being returned to clients. The Mosquitto broker did not fall back to anonymous access; however, 22 eICU devices lost their MQTT sessions simultaneously and could not reconnect for 34 minutes (the duration of the flood plus bcrypt thread-pool recovery). During the 34-minute window, eICU clinicians had no remote visibility into SpO2, ETCO2, or arterial blood pressure for the 22 monitored patients. Two patients required decisions based on values that were last refreshed 34 minutes prior.
actions_taken: The eICU operations centre detected the feed loss at 01:49 UTC. The on-site ICU teams were notified by phone to manually monitor all 22 patients. Upstream rate-limiting at the load balancer was applied at 02:07 UTC. The authentication plugin was redesigned post-incident to use pre-hashed credential lookup (constant-time string compare, not bcrypt) with bcrypt verification deferred to a rate-limited background pool — reducing per-CONNECT auth latency from 120 ms to < 1 ms. The eICU platform was hardened with a 50 CONNECT/s per-IP rate limit on the broker's listener.
outcome: No ePHI exfiltrated. eICU telemetry unavailable for 34 minutes for 22 critically ill patients. Authentication plugin performance bottleneck exploited as a resource-exhaustion vector. Post-incident: auth plugin redesigned; per-IP rate limits applied. Classified as a high-severity availability event.

affected_device: BLE-enabled continuous glucose monitor (CGM) relay (Abbott LibreLink compatible bridge), 6-patient cluster
observed_behaviour: At 14:55 UTC, a rogue BLE advertiser (USB BLE dongle, identified post-incident as a Ubertooth One connected to a laptop in the hospital café adjacent to the clinical ward) began broadcasting BLE advertisement packets impersonating three of the six CGM transmitters by cloning their BLE device addresses (BDA). The LibreLink bridge received forged advertisement packets and initiated connection attempts to the rogue device. The rogue device presented itself as a BLE peripheral but did not implement the Abbott Proprietary BLE GATT service (UUID 0xFCEE) — the bridge's GATT service discovery step returned an empty service table. The bridge's protocol driver aborted the connection attempt and flagged each rogue device as 'incompatible peripheral' in the application log. The three legitimate CGM transmitters whose BDAs were cloned continued to transmit on their authentic channels; the bridge re-acquired them within 12 seconds after clearing the rogue connection attempts. No glucose readings were lost (the bridge buffers 8 hours of readings on-device).
actions_taken: The bridge's 'incompatible peripheral' log event was routed to the SIEM and triggered a 'BLE device impersonation' alert (custom rule) at 14:57 UTC. The SOC used a BLE spectrum analyser to locate the rogue advertiser physically; security staff identified and confiscated the laptop in the café at 15:12 UTC. The device owner was an IT contractor performing an unapproved wireless security assessment. The contractor's access badge was suspended pending HR review. The BLE detection rule was updated to alert within 60 seconds of incompatible-peripheral log events.
outcome: Attack contained. GATT service validation prevented any data exchange with the rogue device. No CGM readings lost; no ePHI disclosed. Detection via SIEM BLE rule in 2 minutes. Physical source located within 17 minutes.

affected_device: BLE-enabled insulin pump controller (Medtronic MiniMed 780G companion app gateway, 4-patient pilot deployment)
observed_behaviour: At 23:02 UTC, a rogue BLE device began advertising using a device address cloned from an enrolled insulin pump (pump serial #IMM-04, patient B). The pilot deployment used an early-integration companion app that implemented BLE Numeric Comparison pairing without user confirmation prompt — a configuration defect where the GATT characteristic for 'pairing confirmation' was auto-accepted if received within 500 ms of the initial pairing request (race condition in the app's threading model). The rogue device sent a pairing request immediately followed by a confirmation frame within 180 ms, triggering the auto-accept path. The companion app established a bonded BLE connection to the rogue device and began forwarding the patient's closed-loop insulin dosing parameters (basal rate schedule, correction factor, ISF) over the rogue GATT channel. The data transfer lasted 4 minutes (23:02–23:06 UTC) until the rogue device terminated the connection. The legitimate pump's actual BLE radio was simultaneously suppressed using a 2.4 GHz narrowband jammer (3 mW, confirmed by post-incident spectral analysis), explaining why the bridge did not receive conflicting advertisements.
actions_taken: The companion app flagged a 'pump disconnected' alert at 23:06 UTC when the rogue device terminated the connection. Nursing staff re-established the legitimate pump connection at 23:11 UTC. Forensic analysis of the companion app's BLE HCI log revealed the auto-accept pairing path. The pilot deployment was suspended on 2024-09-26 pending a fix for the pairing race condition. The vendor issued a patched companion app version (v2.3.1) on 2024-10-08 with a mandatory user confirmation step. A HIPAA breach notification was filed for the one patient (patient B) whose dosing parameters were exfiltrated.
outcome: Insulin dosing parameters (basal rate schedule, correction factor, ISF) for one patient exfiltrated via rogue BLE connection exploiting a pairing auto-accept race condition. ePHI breach confirmed. Pilot suspended; pairing race condition patched in v2.3.1. Jammer used to suppress legitimate device during attack.
attck_technique: T0830 — Adversary-in-the-Middle (BLE pairing exploit) / T0836 — Modify Parameter Settings (dosing data read-out)

affected_device: Smart infusion pump gateway (BD Alaris 8015 PC Unit, 8-pump cluster) and L2 clinical switch (Cisco Catalyst 2960-X)
observed_behaviour: At 11:27 UTC, 16,047 observed ARP flows from 10.10.5.44 (a biomedical IT workstation with a misconfigured ARP proxy script) began poisoning the ARP cache of the clinical switch serving the infusion pump gateway. The ARP rate peaked at 153,124 packets per second during an 18-second burst and sustained at approximately 3,200 pkt/s thereafter. The switch's CAM table was partially corrupted — ARP entries for the infusion pump gateway (10.10.5.10) were overwritten to point to 10.10.5.44's MAC address. For 11 minutes (11:27–11:38 UTC), ePHI-bearing HTTPS telemetry from 6 of the 8 pumps was re-routed to 10.10.5.44. The biomedical workstation was not configured to decrypt TLS traffic — it forwarded the bytes upstream — but the proxy introduced a 200–350 ms latency on each TCP segment. Two pumps with real-time alarm monitoring had their keepalive timers expire due to this latency, triggering 'pump offline' alarms at the nurse station. Nurses investigated and noted the pumps were physically operating normally; the alarms were silenced. No TLS decryption occurred on the proxy.
actions_taken: The infusion pump vendor's gateway health portal detected the latency spike at 11:29 UTC and notified the biomedical engineering team. Investigation identified the ARP poisoning source within 9 minutes. The ARP proxy script on 10.10.5.44 was terminated at 11:38 UTC; the switch's ARP cache was flushed (clear arp-cache) and rebuilt correctly within 60 seconds. Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) was enabled on the clinical VLAN switch post-incident. The biomedical workstation was removed from the clinical VLAN and relegated to a dedicated biomed management VLAN.
outcome: Partial: TLS-encrypted ePHI telemetry from 6 pumps routed through an unintended intermediate host for 11 minutes. No decryption occurred; ePHI confidentiality maintained. Availability degraded: 2 pumps triggered false 'offline' alarms. Root cause: misconfigured ARP proxy on a biomed workstation. Remediation: DAI enabled; biomed VLAN segregated.

affected_device: MQTT broker cluster for hospital-wide alarm aggregation (Halo ION integration, 22 departments)
observed_behaviour: At 13:11 UTC, a MQTT DDoS Publish Flood originated from 31 source IPs (botnet-sourced, spread across 8 countries) targeting the alarm aggregation broker's topic /hospital/alerts/#. Approximately 133,128 observed flows were captured over a 64-second burst at a combined mean publish rate of 1,522.7 messages per second and a peak of 2,522,477 messages per second — consistent with a distributed amplification of the CICIoMT2024 DoS-Publish profile across 31 sources. Payload sizes ranged up to 505,197 bytes each. The broker's topic-rate limiter (Halo ION custom plugin, 500 msg/s per topic wildcard) engaged immediately, dropping the excess publish requests and returning PUBACK with reason code 0x97 (Quota exceeded) to all flooding clients. Legitimate alarm-publishing devices (smoke detectors, nurse-call buttons, patient monitors) continued publishing at their normal rates (< 10 msg/s per device) without interruption. The broker's subscriber for the alarm display console continued to receive all legitimate alarm messages without delay.
actions_taken: The broker's Prometheus rate-limiter metric triggered a PagerDuty alert at 13:11:08 UTC. BGP blackholing of the 31 source IPs was applied by the ISP DDoS mitigation service at 13:14 UTC. Broker operation confirmed normal throughout — zero legitimate alarm messages lost. Post-incident review confirmed topic-rate limiter configuration was effective. No remediation required beyond ISP blackholing.
outcome: No ePHI exposed. Zero legitimate alarm messages lost. Topic-rate limiter held under a 2.5-million-msg/s peak. Alarm aggregation continued uninterrupted for all 22 departments. Attack duration: 3 minutes until ISP blackholing applied.

affected_device: MQTT broker for remote patient monitoring (RPM) platform (cloud-connected, AWS IoT Core bridge), 160 enrolled patients
observed_behaviour: At 04:35 UTC, a distributed MQTT Publish Flood from 28 source IPs targeted the RPM platform's MQTT ingestion broker. 110,940 flows were observed at a peak publish rate of 2,354,314 messages per second. Payload sizes of individual PUBLISH packets reached 505,197 bytes. The broker was running AWS IoT Core's MQTT bridge with no per-topic rate limiting — a configuration that relied on AWS IoT Core's default throttling, which did not apply to bridge-side publishes. The bridge's outbound queue to AWS IoT Core reached 2 GB within 40 seconds, causing the bridge process to request 4 additional GB of heap from the OS. The cloud host (t3.large, 8 GB RAM) entered memory pressure at 04:35:52 UTC and the Linux OOM killer terminated the MQTT bridge process at 04:36:04 UTC. On restart, the bridge re-subscribed to /rpm/# and began processing the queued messages — but the queue held 40 seconds of attacker payloads intermixed with legitimate patient telemetry. The bridge forwarded the entire queue to AWS IoT Core including attacker payloads. AWS IoT Core's IoT rule engine processed each message and triggered a Lambda function that parsed the JSON payload and wrote patient data to DynamoDB. Malformed attacker payloads caused 22 Lambda parsing exceptions, but 4 attacker payloads contained valid JSON that matched the schema — these were written to the DynamoDB patient table under spoofed patient IDs (numeric strings that happened to match real enrolled patient IDs: P-0041, P-0087, P-0118, P-0154). A nurse reviewing DynamoDB-sourced EHR data at 06:22 UTC noticed anomalous glucose values (22.1 mmol/L at 04:36 UTC) for patient P-0041 and initiated a clinical review.
actions_taken: Clinical review at 06:22 UTC identified the anomalous values. IoT security engineer traced the Lambda writes to the attacker payloads at 07:04 UTC. The 4 spurious DynamoDB records were deleted at 07:19 UTC after confirmation they were not legitimate patient data. The patient (P-0041) was contacted; no clinical action had been taken based on the anomalous values. AWS IoT Core bridge was updated with a per-source publish rate limit of 50 msg/s. Payload schema validation was added to the Lambda function (strict JSON schema enforcement, range checks on all clinical values). A risk assessment determined no ePHI was exfiltrated — the harm was integrity corruption, not disclosure.
outcome: Integrity breach: 4 attacker-crafted payloads matching valid patient ID schema were written to the production DynamoDB patient table, inserting spurious clinical data for 4 enrolled patients. No ePHI disclosed externally. Anomalous data detected before clinical action taken. Integrity controls (output validation) absent at Lambda layer. Remediated: per-source rate limiting + strict schema enforcement.
attck_technique: T0814 — Denial of Service / T0832 — Manipulation of Control (data integrity corruption via malformed publish)

affected_device: DICOM-RT treatment planning workstation network interface (Varian Eclipse 16.1, single-NIC UDP/2000 listener)
observed_behaviour: At 16:09 UTC, 78,442 UDP flows from 10.44.2.15 (a compromised lab workstation) targeted the DICOM-RT treatment planning station's UDP port 2000 at a mean rate of 988,213 packets per second (peak 1,644,210 pkt/s) over 6 minutes. The treatment planning station's NIC driver received interrupt saturation within 2 seconds, causing the CPU to spend 97% of cycles in interrupt context. The DICOM-RT session in progress (a radiation oncology physicist reviewing a fractionation plan for a head-and-neck cancer patient) froze and the display became unresponsive at 16:09:07 UTC. The physicist saved a partial draft manually at 16:09:11 UTC and contacted IT. The DICOM-RT session did not autosave during the freeze — 14 minutes of dosimetric optimisation work was lost when the station was rebooted at 16:16 UTC. The patient's radiation plan was in a draft state and had not been approved for treatment; the lost work delayed finalisation by approximately 2.5 hours. No ePHI was transmitted externally during the incident.
actions_taken: IT isolated 10.44.2.15 at 16:14 UTC. The treatment planning station was rebooted at 16:16 UTC. The physicist re-performed the dosimetric optimisation from the last saved checkpoint (16:09:11 UTC). Plan was approved at 18:44 UTC. The treatment appointment for the next morning was maintained. Post-incident: UDP rate limiting on the DICOM VLAN (500 pkt/s per source) was applied; DICOM-RT autosave was enabled (60-second interval, previously disabled by local preference).
outcome: No ePHI exfiltrated. Partial impact: 14 minutes of unsaved dosimetric work lost; patient radiation plan approval delayed 2.5 hours. Treatment appointment maintained. Root cause: missing UDP rate limit on DICOM VLAN and disabled autosave. Both remediated post-incident.

affected_device: Telestroke consultation server (Teladoc Health InTouch Elite, HIPAA-BAA covered SaaS bridge), single-site gateway node
observed_behaviour: At 22:48 UTC, a concentrated ICMP flood from 172.31.9.44 (compromised on-premises server) directed 25,917 observed flows at the telestroke consultation gateway at a mean rate of 927 pkt/s (peak 38,412 pkt/s). The gateway ran a local WebRTC relay (coturn v4.6.2) that consumed all available socket-read capacity while processing ICMP-driven interrupt load, causing the WebRTC video session between an emergency physician and a remote stroke neurologist to freeze at 22:48:41 UTC. The neurologist was evaluating MRI images transmitted via the WebRTC session for a 68-year-old patient with suspected ischemic stroke (NIH Stroke Scale 12). The session froze during image transmission — 9 of 14 MRI slides had been transmitted. The neurologist was unable to evaluate the remaining 5 slides (diffusion-weighted imaging showing early ischemic territory extent). The neurologist made a treatment recommendation — tPA administration — based on the 9 available slides. The on-site physician administered tPA at 23:04 UTC. A retrospective review of the 5 untransmitted DWI slides on 2024-12-12 showed a larger ischemic territory (ASPECTS score 5) that would likely have changed the treatment decision to mechanical thrombectomy rather than tPA alone. The patient had an adverse outcome (symptomatic haemorrhagic transformation on day 3).
actions_taken: The coturn relay recovered at 22:54 UTC when the ICMP flood subsided. The neurologist reconnected and reviewed the remaining 5 MRI slides at 22:56 UTC — 52 minutes after tPA administration. The ICMP flood source (172.31.9.44) was identified as a misconfigured network monitoring probe and corrected; no malicious intent was established. A post-incident clinical review initiated by the stroke team examined whether the treatment decision would have differed with complete imaging. The adverse outcome review remains open as of filing date.
outcome: Telestroke consultation session frozen mid-imaging during acute stroke evaluation; 5 critical DWI slides not transmitted before treatment decision. Patient received tPA; subsequent imaging suggested thrombectomy may have been preferable. Adverse outcome under clinical review. ePHI (MRI images, neurologist consultation notes) were not exfiltrated. ICMP rate-limiting added to the WebRTC relay subnet. Clinical-impact severity: high.

affected_device: Secure messaging gateway for clinical communications (TigerConnect Enterprise, TCP/443 TLS)
observed_behaviour: At 09:33 UTC, a distributed SYN flood from 67 source IPs generated 199,390 observed flows at a mean packet rate of 297,810 per second and a peak of 16,777,216 per second (matching CICIoMT2024 DDoS-SYN1). The TigerConnect gateway's SYN cookie implementation handled the flood correctly — no half-open connections accumulated — but the sheer volume caused the TCP kernel's per-CPU receive queue (RPS) to overflow on 3 of 8 cores. Packets assigned to those cores were dropped, including some legitimate TLS ClientHello messages. Fourteen physicians attempting to send time-sensitive clinical messages (lab result alerts, imaging consult requests) during the 12-minute outage received 'connection failed' errors on their mobile apps. No message content was exposed — TLS was never established for any attacking SYN. However, two physicians reverted to unsecured SMS for urgent communication during the outage, transmitting patient MRN and diagnosis information via unencrypted channel — a HIPAA-non-compliant fallback that was not sanctioned by policy.
actions_taken: DDoS mitigation (Cloudflare Spectrum) was activated at 09:38 UTC and absorbed the SYN flood at the edge. Service was fully restored at 09:45 UTC. The two SMS messages were identified during post-incident review; the transmitting physicians were counselled. A policy update was issued: approved fallback is encrypted voice call (not SMS) when TigerConnect is unavailable. The IT security team reviewed the RPS queue tuning and re-allocated CPU affinity to balance TLS-initiation load.
outcome: Partial: two physicians transmitted ePHI (MRN + diagnosis) via unencrypted SMS due to perceived unavailability of the secure messaging platform during the DDoS window. No TLS-protected ePHI was accessed by the attacker. Policy violation documented and addressed; physicians counselled. Cloudflare mitigation service activated and retained.

affected_device: Bedside monitor DTLS gateway (GE Healthcare CARESCAPE B650, 18-bed ICU, UDP/4739)
observed_behaviour: At 15:22 UTC, 206,170 UDP flows from 52 source IPs targeted port 4739 (IPFIX/DTLS telemetry export) of the CARESCAPE gateway at a mean rate of 741,818 pkt/s. The DTLS handshake state machine was overwhelmed — the gateway's DTLS cookie mechanism (RFC 6347 HelloVerifyRequest) was present but the cookie computation used a static secret that had not been rotated in 14 months (key rotation policy: 90 days, unimplemented). The static secret was not compromised, but the static nature reduced the cookie entropy below the recommended 128 bits. The DTLS listener processed 4,388 concurrent HelloVerifyRequest exchanges simultaneously, exhausting the gateway's UDP socket buffer (8 MB). Legitimate DTLS sessions from 18 CARESCAPE monitors were disrupted for 9 minutes. During this period, bedside ICU telemetry (HR, SpO2, ABP, ETCO2) was not transmitted to the central station; nursing staff relied on bedside display only. No DTLS session was successfully established by the attacker (cookie verification rejected all forged ClientHellos). ePHI in transit was not decrypted.
actions_taken: NOC applied upstream BGP rate-limiting at 15:26 UTC; DTLS flood subsided. Gateway DTLS sessions re-established within 60 seconds. DTLS cookie secret was immediately rotated post-incident; a 90-day automatic rotation job was implemented. UDP socket buffer increased from 8 MB to 64 MB to handle burst DTLS exchange volume. A finding was filed in the risk register regarding the unimplemented key rotation policy.
outcome: No ePHI decrypted or exfiltrated. DTLS integrity held; all attacker ClientHellos rejected by cookie verification. 9-minute ICU telemetry disruption. Partial control gap: DTLS cookie secret rotation policy was non-compliant (14 months vs. 90-day requirement). Remediated: automated rotation implemented.

affected_device: Infusion pump fleet management server (B. Braun Space Station, 72 pumps, TCP/80 HTTP and TCP/443 HTTPS)
observed_behaviour: At 11:14 UTC, 83,981 observed network flows from 10.7.8.33 (a clinical engineering workstation running a Nmap scheduled task inadvertently left active after an asset inventory project) scanned all ports on the infusion pump management server subnet over 77 minutes. Mean flow rate was 88.8 pkt/s (peak 141,582.6 pkt/s). The scan identified that the pump management server responded on TCP/80 (HTTP, non-redirecting to HTTPS) in addition to TCP/443. The HTTP listener on port 80 served an unprotected /status endpoint returning JSON with pump count, firmware version, and the last successful sync timestamp — no ePHI, but the firmware version (B. Braun SpaceStation FW 012U) was sufficient to identify a known advisory (BSI-2022-0318) for unauthenticated configuration read via a specially crafted GET /api/pump/{id}/config request. The advisory noted that ePHI (infusion schedule) was accessible via this endpoint on FW versions ≤012V. The scan result and the advisory were correlated by the clinical engineering team 6 days later during routine review.
actions_taken: TCP/80 was immediately disabled (redirect-only to HTTPS) on 2024-08-12. The /api/pump/{id}/config endpoint was confirmed to require authentication on FW 012U — the advisory affected only FW ≤012T, which this deployment had already patched. No ePHI exposure was confirmed. The scheduled Nmap task was removed from the clinical engineering workstation. Port scanning within clinical VLANs was added to the approved-activity register requiring change-advisory board (CAB) approval.
outcome: No ePHI exposed. Unprotected HTTP status endpoint disclosed firmware version (no ePHI in payload). CVE assessment confirmed FW 012U was not vulnerable to the advisory. Partial gap: HTTP port 80 active alongside HTTPS without redirect, exposing unauthenticated status endpoint. Remediated: port 80 disabled; scanning policy formalised.
attck_technique: T0840 — Network Sniffing / T0888 — Remote Services Exploitation (pre-assessment)

affected_device: Anaesthesia workstation cluster (3 Mindray A9, TCP/22 SFTP configuration backup port)
observed_behaviour: At 08:04 UTC, 16,832 observed flows from 192.0.2.88 (a Tor exit node) targeted the hospital's DMZ at a mean rate of 148.1 pkt/s (peak 90,366.6 pkt/s) over 31 minutes. The OS fingerprint scan probed all three anaesthesia workstations and returned 'VxWorks 6.9' — the RTOS embedded in the Mindray A9 platform — from TCP window scale, TTL=64, and selective-acknowledgement options. The OS fingerprint was visible because SFTP port 22 was inadvertently accessible at the DMZ firewall (a configuration ticket had removed the SFTP allowance from the IoMT VLAN rule but missed the DMZ edge rule). VxWorks 6.9 is associated with multiple published CVEs (CVE-2019-12255 through CVE-2019-12264, 'URGENT/11'), all of which were patched in Mindray FW 2.3.1. The workstations were running FW 2.3.1; the CVEs were not exploitable. No connection was established on port 22 beyond the fingerprinting probe.
actions_taken: The DMZ firewall misconfiguration was identified during the weekly firewall rule review on 2024-03-26. The erroneous SFTP allowance at the DMZ edge was removed. OS fingerprinting telltales (TCP window scale, IPID) were randomised by enabling the kernel's tcp_timestamps and ip_no_pmtu_disc options. No exploitation was confirmed. The Mindray FW version audit confirmed all three workstations were on FW 2.3.1 (URGENT/11 patched).
outcome: OS fingerprint disclosed (VxWorks 6.9) via DMZ misconfiguration, but associated CVEs were patched. No exploitation, no ePHI exposure. DMZ firewall rule corrected. OS fingerprint obfuscation enabled. Classified as a near-miss requiring no breach notification.

affected_device: Ventilator management portal (Hamilton Medical HAMILTON-G5, web admin, TCP/443)
observed_behaviour: At 02:11 UTC, 2,173 observed flows from 198.51.100.77 targeted the ventilator management portal at a mean rate of 97.5 pkt/s (peak 11,401.6 pkt/s) over 22 minutes. Nmap + Nuclei templates identified: (1) Tomcat 8.5.73 with CVE-2021-33037 (partial request smuggling, CVSS 5.3), (2) outdated jQuery 1.12.4 with CVE-2019-11358 (prototype pollution), and (3) a directory traversal in the web app's report download handler (/reports/download?file=../../etc/passwd) that returned 200 OK with the /etc/passwd file contents. The directory traversal was exploited in the same session at 02:28 UTC: the attacker downloaded /etc/shadow (readable due to a misconfigured umask), /opt/hamilton/config/db.properties (containing the MySQL username and password for the portal database), and subsequently connected to MySQL on localhost via a SSH tunnel established using a weak RSA-1024 key found in /root/.ssh/authorised_keys. The MySQL portal database contained current ventilator configuration parameters and 89 patient records (MRN, admission date, current PEEP/FiO2 settings, attending physician).
actions_taken: The portal was taken offline at 06:44 UTC when morning clinical staff noticed the web interface was returning error pages (MySQL connection failure after the attacker deleted a table). Forensic analysis completed by 2024-04-17. 89 patient records confirmed exfiltrated. Directory traversal was patched by removing the file download handler and replacing with a signed token-based download URL. RSA-1024 key replaced with Ed25519. MySQL port restricted to localhost only (no SSH tunnel capability). HIPAA breach notification filed for 89 patients.
outcome: 89 patient ePHI records (MRN, ventilator settings, attending physician) exfiltrated via directory traversal and MySQL credential exposure. Vulnerability scan was the reconnaissance step enabling the exploit. Breach confirmed. Portal offline 9+ hours during forensics. Breach notification filed under 45 CFR §164.400.
attck_technique: T0888 — Remote Services Exploitation (directory traversal → credential exposure → DB exfiltration)

affected_device: MQTT broker for fetal monitoring (CTG) integration (Philips Avalon wireless CTG, 4 active patients)
observed_behaviour: At 20:17 UTC, the CTG MQTT broker received 5,130 malformed MQTT PUBLISH packets — matching the CICIoMT2024 MQTT-Malformed_Data flow count — from 10.6.9.200 (a biomedical workstation with a faulty firmware update utility that generated malformed MQTT frames as a side-effect). Each PUBLISH packet carried a REMAINING LENGTH field encoded as a 4-byte value with the continuation bit incorrectly set on the final byte (0x80 flag set), causing the broker's length decoder to read an additional 128 bytes past the actual payload boundary. The broker (Mosquitto 2.0.11) returned PUBACK without error — the length decoder silently truncated overlong reads. The overread bytes came from adjacent TCP receive buffer contents, which in 6 cases contained partial JSON from prior legitimate CTG PUBLISH messages. These 6 partial JSON fragments were concatenated with the attacker's nominal payload and forwarded to the CTG subscriber. The subscriber's JSON parser encountered unexpected CTG data values (FHR 312 bpm, an impossible reading) and logged parse errors but did not discard the records — it wrote the impossible values to the fetal monitoring EHR module.
actions_taken: A midwife reviewing the CTG trace at 20:31 UTC noticed the impossible FHR readings and immediately escalated. Clinical assessment confirmed the four patients' actual FHR values were normal (confirmed by bedside Doppler). The 6 spurious EHR entries were flagged as 'data quality error — pending review' and not used clinically. The Mosquitto REMAINING LENGTH decoder was patched by upgrading to Mosquitto 2.0.15. A range-validation filter was added to the CTG subscriber (valid FHR: 50–210 bpm; values outside this range are rejected and alerted). The biomedical workstation's firmware update utility was debugged and the malformed-frame generation was corrected.
outcome: No ePHI disclosed externally. Partial integrity failure: 6 spurious impossible FHR values written to the fetal monitoring EHR module. Detected and quarantined before clinical use. Root cause: MQTT remaining-length silent truncation + absent subscriber input validation. Mosquitto updated; range validation added.
attck_technique: T0832 — Manipulation of Control (indirect — malformed message integrity failure)

affected_device: Wireless ECG telemetry gateway (Philips PIIC iX, 16-bed telemetry unit, L2 Wi-Fi VLAN)
observed_behaviour: At 14:38 UTC, 16,047 observed ARP flows from 10.20.1.77 (a guest-network device that had laterally moved through a misconfigured VLAN trunk) began poisoning the ARP cache of the telemetry VLAN gateway at a peak rate of 153,124 pkt/s. Within 3 seconds the gateway's ARP entry for the PIIC iX access point (10.20.1.10) was overwritten with 10.20.1.77's MAC. The access point sent a DHCP probe (RFC 3927 conflict detection) that conflicted with the rogue ARP entry; the conflict detection triggered the PIIC iX's 'ARP conflict detected' alarm at 14:38:07 UTC. Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on the telemetry VLAN switch had been enabled 3 months prior and maintained a DHCP snooping binding table. DAI detected the unsolicited ARP reply from 10.20.1.77, classified it as an ARP spoofing attempt, and dropped all subsequent ARP frames from that MAC address on the telemetry VLAN. The legitimate ARP entry for 10.20.1.10 was preserved. ECG telemetry continued without interruption.
actions_taken: The DAI drop event was logged and generated a SIEM alert at 14:38:09 UTC. The source device (10.20.1.77) was traced to a guest user's personal laptop connected to the wrong VLAN via an unsecured switch port in a patient bay. The port was shut down at 14:40 UTC. VLAN trunk misconfiguration was corrected. No telemetry disruption; no ePHI exposed. The PIIC iX conflict-detection alarm was cleared.
outcome: Attack fully contained. DAI dropped all rogue ARP frames within 3 seconds of onset. ECG telemetry uninterrupted. No ePHI exposed. VLAN misconfiguration corrected. DAI confirmed as effective control for ARP spoofing on clinical Wi-Fi VLANs.

affected_device: BLE-enabled smart pill dispenser (Hero Health dispenser, 12 enrolled outpatients, BLE 5.0)
observed_behaviour: At 11:03 UTC, a rogue BLE device advertising under a cloned device address (BDA matching enrolled patient P-0067's pill dispenser) established a connection with the dispenser's companion app running on a hospital-owned tablet in the pharmacy consultation room. The rogue device passed the GATT service UUID check (UUID 0xA8B3FBE8, cloned from a captured BLE advertisement). The companion app's pairing implementation used 'Just Works' pairing mode (no MITM protection) — a configuration permitted for BLE 4.2 legacy devices but inappropriate for the BLE 5.0 pill dispenser which supported LE Secure Connections. The rogue device requested 'Just Works' downgrade and it was accepted. The attacker's rogue device then read the pill dispenser's GATT characteristic for 'scheduled doses' (UUID 0xC7E70012), which returned P-0067's weekly medication schedule (drug names, doses, times). The schedule is ePHI — it identifies a specific patient's medication regimen.
actions_taken: The pharmacy technician noticed the tablet's companion app showed 'connected' to a dispenser whose physical device was not in the room and alerted IT. affected_device: Network time protocol (NTP) server for IoMT synchronisation (stratum-2, UDP/123)
observed_behaviour: At 03:41 UTC, 194,938 ICMP flows from 39 source IPs produced a peak rate of 1,321,810 pkt/s against the IoMT NTP server (matching CICIoMT2024 DDoS-ICMP1 profile). The NTP server (ntpd 4.2.8p15) continued to respond to NTP requests throughout — its UDP/123 listener was unaffected by ICMP load, which was handled by a separate interrupt-driven path. However, the ICMP flood consumed 68% of the server's NIC bandwidth (1 Gbps link). Seven IoMT devices whose NTP polling interval exceeded 128 seconds did not receive NTP responses during the 9-minute flood because their NTP packets were queued behind ICMP interrupt processing; these devices drifted 0.8–1.4 seconds. Post-flood, all 7 devices re-synced within 2 minutes. No TLS sessions were impacted (drift < 3 seconds). No ePHI in transit was disrupted.
actions_taken: Perimeter ICMP rate-limiting (1,000 pkt/s per source) was applied at 03:44 UTC. NTP server recovered fully by 03:51 UTC. All 7 devices re-synced by 03:53 UTC. Post-incident: ICMP rate-limiting was made a permanent perimeter rule; NTP server was moved behind a load balancer with DDoS scrubbing. Separate NTP VIP added for IoMT VLAN to isolate timing traffic from internet-facing interfaces.
outcome: No ePHI exposed. 7 IoMT devices drifted 0.8–1.4 seconds during 9-minute outage; no TLS failures. All re-synced post-flood. Perimeter ICMP rate-limiting made permanent. NTP infrastructure hardened with scrubbing and IoMT-dedicated VIP.

affected_device: HL7 interface engine (Mirth Connect 4.3.0, TCP/2575 MLLP) for lab result routing, 6 downstream EHR consumers
observed_behaviour: At 05:22 UTC, a distributed TCP flood from 47 source IPs generated 202,311 observed flows at a mean rate of 741,818 pkt/s and peak of 2,097,152 pkt/s (matching the CICIoMT2024 DDoS-TCP1 profile) against the Mirth Connect MLLP listener on TCP/2575. actions_taken: ISP BGP blackholing was applied at 05:28 UTC; the MLLP listener recovered at 05:36 UTC. Mirth Connect ring buffer overrun was identified at 05:38 UTC. The lab informatics team initiated a manual reconciliation process — printed lab reports were cross-checked against EHR entries. The 312 missing ORU messages were manually re-entered by 08:15 UTC. No ePHI was exposed externally. Post-incident: Mirth Connect ring buffer increased to 2 GB; a persistent disk-backed overflow queue (Apache Kafka) was introduced to prevent future message loss; DDoS mitigation scrubbing was added upstream of the MLLP listener.
outcome: No ePHI exfiltrated. 312 HL7 lab result messages (88 patients) lost from Mirth ring buffer overflow; manually recovered from printed reports by 08:15 UTC. No patient care delay documented. Integrity impact: 14-minute gap in EHR lab result availability. Buffer capacity and persistent queue remediated post-incident.
